**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |

| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| **Physical State (298 K, 1 atm)** | Phase | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (−423.15 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (−434.69 °F) |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat (gas, 1 bar) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.449 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Heat of fusion | 0.000 kJ mol⁻¹ (negligible) |
| | Thermal conductivity | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Viscosity | 8.76 × 10⁻⁶ Pa s |
| | Speed of sound | 1270 m s⁻¹ |
| | Refractive index | 1.000132 (visible light) |
| | Dielectric constant | 1.000132 |
| | Magnetic susceptibility | –2.7 × 10⁻⁶ cm³ g⁻¹ |
| **Chemical Properties** | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (H₂) |
| | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds; H₂ is a diatomic molecule with a single σ bond |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, acids with nonmetals, and oxidizes to water or oxides |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (H⁺ donor) in aqueous solution; forms hydronium (H₃O⁺) |
| | Redox behavior | Reducing agent (e.g., H₂ + O₂ → H₂O); oxidized to H⁺ in acids |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Spectral lines | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) |
| | Ionization potential | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Dissociation energy (H₂) | 4.478 eV (≈ 432 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Bond length (H₂) | 0.741 Å |
| | Dipole moment | 0 (homonuclear diatomic) |
| | Polarizability | 0.666 Å³ |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ of natural hydrogen |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion research |
| | Isotopic effects | Deuterium forms stronger bonds (e.g., D₂O has higher boiling point) |
| **Physical Behavior** | Diffusion coefficient (air) | ~0.2 cm² s⁻¹ at 25 °C |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 g L⁻¹ at 20 °C (≈ 0.0006 mol L⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in hydrocarbons | Higher than in water (e.g., 0.5 mol L⁻¹ in n‑hexane) |

| | Triple point | –259.16 °C, 0.00022 MPa |
| **Applications & Roles** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells) | Produces electricity via H₂ + O₂ → H₂O |
| | Chemical feedstock | Used to produce ammonia (Haber process), methanol, etc. |
| | Space propulsion | Liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen as rocket propellant |
| | Metallurgy | Reduces metal oxides to metals (e.g., steelmaking) |
| | Nuclear fusion | Deuterium–tritium fusion (D + T → He + n + 17.6 MeV) |
| | Astrophysics | Primary element in stars; fusion in stellar cores produces helium |
| | Spectroscopy | Hydrogen spectral lines used for calibration and astrophysical diagnostics |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive limits 4–75 % (v/v) in air |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but inhalation of high concentrations can displace oxygen (asphyxiation risk) |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders (up to 700 bar) or cryogenic tanks (liquid H₂ at –253 °C) |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion product (water); no greenhouse gases emitted |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and a single stable isotope (protium) plus two rare isotopes (deuterium, tritium).
- **It is a gas at room temperature** with an extremely low density and a very low boiling point.
- **Chemically, it is highly reactive**: it forms hydrides with metals, reacts with acids, and burns readily to produce water.
- **Its isotopes have distinct physical properties** (e.g., deuterium’s higher boiling point) and are crucial in nuclear fusion research.
- **Hydrogen plays a pivotal role in energy technologies** (fuel cells, rocket propellants) and in the chemistry of life and industry.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
